distillate: A GWAS tests every common SNP, one at a time, for association with a trait, and calls a hit only below p = 5×10⁻⁸. One SNP with allele counts 220/180 in 200 cases and 180/220 in 200 controls gives OR = 1.49 and p = 0.0047, and would need about 1,500 people to clear that bar. In a simulated scan of 10,000 people with ten true risk loci (OR 1.10–1.40), only the three largest effects cross the line, and leaving out ancestry covariates inflates every test statistic (λ = 1.92 instead of 1.09) and shifts which loci look significant.
model: [Mistral Large 4, Claude Opus 5.5]
---

A **genome-wide association study** (GWAS) asks the same question of every common genetic variant: in this population, does carrying this allele go with the trait? The method took off in 2005–2007, when the first robust hit appeared (complement factor H in age-related macular degeneration, Klein et al., 2005) and the Wellcome Trust Case Control Consortium ran 14,000 cases of seven diseases against 3,000 shared controls on a 500,000-SNP array (WTCCC, 2007). Every published association is now indexed in the [GWAS Catalog](https://www.ebi.ac.uk/gwas/) (MacArthur et al., 2017).

The note works at two scales. First, one SNP in a small case-control study, to show the test itself:

| | value |
| --- | --- |
| design | 200 cases, 200 controls |
| one SNP, allele counts | cases: A = 220, a = 180; controls: A = 180, a = 220 |
| significance bar | $p < 5 \times 10^{-8}$ (genome-wide) |

Then a whole simulated scan, to show what the output of a real GWAS looks like and what goes wrong in it:

| | value |
| --- | --- |
| people | 10,000 (2,017 cases, 7,983 controls; prevalence about 20%) |
| SNPs | 6,000 on 22 chromosomes, correlated with their neighbours (LD) |
| ancestry | 70% group A, 30% group B, allele frequencies differing with $F_{ST} = 0.01$ |
| confounder | group B has more disease for non-genetic reasons (log-odds +0.5) |
| true risk loci | 10, one SNP each, odds ratios 1.10, 1.12, 1.15, 1.18, 1.20, 1.22, 1.25, 1.30, 1.35, 1.40 |
| test | logistic regression per SNP, without and with 4 principal components |

## The single-SNP test

For one SNP, the data collapse into a 2×2 table of allele counts, and the **allelic odds ratio** compares the odds of carrying allele A in cases and in controls:

$$
\mathrm{OR} = \frac{220/180}{180/220} = \frac{220 \times 220}{180 \times 180} = 1.49
$$

Under the null hypothesis of no association, each cell's expected count $E$ is its row total times its column total divided by the total, here $200 \times 400 / 800 = 200$ for every cell. The **chi-square** statistic sums the squared deviations of the observed counts $O$:

$$
\chi^2 = \sum \frac{(O - E)^2}{E} = 4 \times \frac{20^2}{200} = 8.0
$$

With 1 degree of freedom, $\chi^2 = 8.0$ gives $p = 0.0047$. On its own that would count as suggestive. In a genome-wide scan it is nothing, because tests like it are run a million times. The test also assumes the case and control labels are right; when they come from diagnosis codes in health records, they often aren't, and the [medical codes note](note:medical-codes) works out what that costs in odds ratio and sample size.

The allele-count table treats the 800 alleles as independent draws, which holds only under Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium. Real pipelines instead regress the trait on genotype dosage (0, 1 or 2 copies of A) with covariates: logistic regression for a disease, linear for a quantitative trait. For one SNP without covariates the two give nearly the same answer, and the regression form is what the simulated scan below uses. In practice it is run with tools such as PLINK (Chang et al., 2015) or REGENIE (Mbatchou et al., 2021).

In R, the 2×2 test is a few lines:

```r
# One SNP, allele counts in 200 cases and 200 controls
tab <- matrix(c(220, 180,
                180, 220), nrow = 2, byrow = TRUE,
              dimnames = list(c("case", "control"), c("A", "a")))
OR <- (tab["case", "A"] * tab["control", "a"]) / (tab["case", "a"] * tab["control", "A"])
test <- chisq.test(tab, correct = FALSE)       # Pearson chi-square, 1 df
cat(sprintf("OR = %.2f, chi2 = %.1f, p = %.4f, -log10(p) = %.2f\n",
            OR, test$statistic, test$p.value, -log10(test$p.value)))
chi2_thr <- qchisq(5e-8, df = 1, lower.tail = FALSE)  # genome-wide bar
people <- (sum(tab) / 2) * chi2_thr / test$statistic   # chi2 scales with sample size
cat(sprintf("p < 5e-8 needs chi2 = %.1f, about %.0f people at this effect size\n",
            chi2_thr, round(people, -2)))
```

which prints:

```
OR = 1.49, chi2 = 8.0, p = 0.0047, -log10(p) = 2.33
p < 5e-8 needs chi2 = 29.7, about 1500 people at this effect size
```

## Multiple testing and the 5×10⁻⁸ bar

A GWAS tests around a million common SNPs, and more after imputation, so even with no true effects about $0.05 \times 10^6 = 50{,}000$ of them would reach $p < 0.05$. Because nearby SNPs are correlated, the genome of European-ancestry populations holds roughly a million *independent* common-variant tests, and a Bonferroni correction for that many gives the field's standard bar of $p < 5 \times 10^{-8}$, or $-\log_{10} p > 7.3$ (Pe'er et al., 2008).

For 1 degree of freedom, $p = 5 \times 10^{-8}$ corresponds to $\chi^2 = 29.7$. At a fixed effect size $\chi^2$ grows roughly in proportion to the sample size, so the toy SNP (OR 1.49, $\chi^2 = 8.0$ from 400 people) would need about $29.7 / 8.0 = 3.7$ times the sample, roughly 1,500 people, to clear the bar. A p-value is not an effect size: in samples of hundreds of thousands, the typical hit for a common disease has an odds ratio of only about 1.05 to 1.2. That is why GWAS samples grew from thousands (WTCCC) to hundreds of thousands (UK Biobank, about 500,000 participants; Bycroft et al., 2018).

## A whole scan, simulated

One SNP can't show what a GWAS produces. The R script at the end of the note simulates the second table: 10,000 people, two ancestry groups, ten true risk SNPs, and LD made by letting each chromosome's alleles follow a correlated random walk, so neighbouring SNPs share information and a causal SNP drags its neighbours along. The genome is compressed: 6,000 SNPs stand in for millions, and the odds ratios are larger than typical real ones so that a 10,000-person study can find some of them. The results are read from two plots.

A **Manhattan plot** puts every SNP at its position along the genome and its $-\log_{10} p$ on the vertical axis, so strong associations stand up as towers:

*Manhattan plot of the simulated scan, adjusted for 4 principal components. Chromosomes alternate in shade; accent ticks on the axis mark the ten true risk SNPs, and accent points are the three that cross the genome-wide line (5×10⁻⁸, 7.3 on the vertical axis). The tower on chromosome 6 is a true locus that falls just short.*

Three things show up here that a single SNP can't show.

**Hits come as towers, not points.** Each true locus lifts a column of neighbouring SNPs, because those SNPs are in LD with the causal one. On chromosome 16 the causal SNP reaches $p = 1.6 \times 10^{-14}$, and SNPs a few positions away still reach $10^{-4}$ to $10^{-5}$. In real data, a tower like this spans tens to hundreds of kilobases and can contain dozens of genes, which is why the lead SNP of a locus is a pointer, not an answer.

**Most true effects are missed.** Only the three largest effects cross the line: chromosome 13 (OR 1.30, $p = 1.2 \times 10^{-8}$), chromosome 16 (OR 1.35, $p = 1.6 \times 10^{-14}$) and chromosome 19 (OR 1.40, $p = 3.1 \times 10^{-9}$). Chromosomes 6 (OR 1.18) and 11 (OR 1.25) both stop at $p = 2.6 \times 10^{-7}$ and $2.4 \times 10^{-7}$, and the four smallest effects are lost in the background. Which of two similar effects crosses the line is partly luck: here the OR 1.18 locus beat the OR 1.20 and 1.22 ones, because sampling noise and allele frequency matter as much as the odds ratio at this sample size. A real study at this size reports three loci and says nothing about the other seven, and the effect sizes of the three it does report are biased upward, the **winner's curse**, because they were selected for having come out large.

**The line is the bar for a real genome.** With only 6,000 tests, a Bonferroni bar for this simulated genome would be $0.05 / 6{,}000 = 8.3 \times 10^{-6}$. The plot keeps $5 \times 10^{-8}$ because that is the bar the scan would face in a real genome of a million independent tests.

## Population stratification and the QQ plot

The main source of false positives is **population stratification**: if cases and controls differ in ancestry, any allele whose frequency differs between ancestries looks associated with the disease. In the simulation, group B has more disease for reasons that have nothing to do with the SNPs, and the two groups' allele frequencies have drifted apart, by about 4 to 6 percentage points at a typical SNP. A SNP with no effect at all then looks like a risk allele if it happens to be more common in B.

The standard fix is to add the top **principal components** (PCs) of the genotype matrix as covariates (Price et al., 2006). The first PC of the simulated genotypes separates the two groups almost perfectly (correlation 0.99 with group membership), so adjusting for it removes most of the confounding. Real analyses add age, sex and genotyping batch as well.

A **QQ plot** shows whether it worked. It sorts the observed p-values and plots them against the values expected if no SNP had any effect. Under the null the points follow the diagonal; true hits peel off at the top right. Inflation is summarized by the **genomic-control** factor $\lambda$, the median observed $\chi^2$ divided by its expected median under the null, 0.455 (Devlin and Roeder, 1999):

  <text x="64.1" y="36.6" font-size="12" fill="currentColor"><tspan style="fill: var(--muted)">●</tspan> no covariates, λ = 1.92</text>
  <text x="64.1" y="55.9" font-size="12" fill="currentColor"><tspan style="fill: var(--accent)">●</tspan> 4 PCs, λ = 1.09</text>
</svg>

*QQ plot of the same 6,000 tests. Without covariates (grey) the whole curve lifts off the diagonal; with 4 PCs (accent) it follows the diagonal until the true loci break away.*

Without covariates, $\lambda = 1.92$: the typical test statistic is nearly double what it should be, and every p-value in the genome is too small. With 4 PCs, $\lambda = 1.09$. Counting only SNPs more than 40 positions from any causal SNP, the values are 1.84 and 1.03, so the remaining 1.09 is mostly true signal spread across the towers by LD, not leftover confounding.

Stratification doesn't only add false hits; it shifts real ones in both directions. Without covariates, eight SNPs at four loci cross the line. The causal SNP on chromosome 6, whose risk allele is 7 points more common in group B, reaches $p = 6.0 \times 10^{-10}$, but only $2.6 \times 10^{-7}$ once ancestry is accounted for: part of its raw signal was the extra disease in group B. On chromosome 13 the risk allele is 6 points *less* common in B, and ancestry hides it: $p = 8.5 \times 10^{-7}$ raw, $1.2 \times 10^{-8}$ adjusted. A study that skipped the PCs would report the wrong set of loci with no way to tell from the Manhattan plot alone.

That is also why $\lambda$ is a blunt tool in real data. A truly polygenic trait, with thousands of small effects in LD with many SNPs, inflates $\lambda$ with no confounding at all, and the larger the study, the larger the inflation. **LD score regression** separates the two (Bulik-Sullivan et al., 2015): it regresses each SNP's $\chi^2$ on how much LD the SNP has with its neighbours. True polygenic signal grows with LD; confounding doesn't, so it shows up in the intercept instead of the slope.

## Genotyping, imputation, meta-analysis

Arrays measure about 0.5–2 million SNPs directly (WTCCC used the Affymetrix 500K). Because SNPs are correlated, the measured ones can **impute** the rest against a reference panel of sequenced genomes such as the 1000 Genomes Project (2015). Larger panels such as HRC and TOPMed now give imputed dosages (0–2, fractional where uncertain) for tens of millions of variants. Imputation works for common variants; rare ones, below about 0.5% frequency, are poorly tagged and need sequencing. Separate cohorts are then combined by inverse-variance-weighted meta-analysis of each SNP's effect size and standard error, which is how most published GWAS reach hundreds of thousands of people.

## From hits to biology

A lead SNP is rarely the causal one: it is the best-tagged member of a tower. In the simulation the causal SNP is known, and at the chromosome 13 locus the raw scan's lead SNP is its neighbour, not the causal SNP itself. **Fine-mapping** methods such as SuSiE (Wang et al., 2020) turn a tower into a *credible set*, a small group of SNPs that contains the causal one with a stated probability. Follow-up then links loci to genes, for example through expression QTLs, variants that change a gene's expression in some tissue (GTEx Consortium, 2017). Discovery effect sizes shrink on replication because of the winner's curse described above. The hits and their effect sizes also feed the [polygenic risk scores note](note:polygenic-risk-scores) and the instruments of [Mendelian randomization](note:mendelian-randomization).

## What GWAS showed about architecture

Beyond single loci, GWAS measured how traits are built. SNP-based heritability, the share of trait variance that all common SNPs together explain (GCTA; Yang et al., 2011), turned out to be large for many traits, so much of the "missing heritability" sits in many SNPs each too small to cross 5×10⁻⁸ at the sample sizes of the time. Height is the clearest case: a GWAS of 5.4 million people found about 12,000 independent signals that together account for about 40% of height variance in European-ancestry samples, nearly all of the common-SNP heritability (Yengo et al., 2022). The simulated scan, with seven of ten true loci missed at 10,000 people, is the same story in miniature.

Most GWAS samples are of European ancestry. Allele frequencies and LD patterns differ between ancestries, so loci are missed in under-studied populations, and results transfer poorly: the same height SNPs account for only about 10–20% of variance in other ancestries (Yengo et al., 2022). The PRS note follows this through to risk scores.

## The simulated scan in R

The full simulation and scan. It needs the `irlba` package for a fast PCA and takes about two minutes:

```r
set.seed(2026)
N <- 10000; rho <- 0.9; Fst <- 0.01   # people, LD between neighbouring SNPs, ancestry drift
chr <- rep(1:22, times = round(6000 * (23 - 1:22) / 253))  # 6,000 SNPs, longer chromosomes first
M <- length(chr)
pop <- rbinom(N, 1, 0.3)                         # 70% ancestry A, 30% ancestry B
p0 <- runif(M, 0.05, 0.5)                        # ancestral allele frequencies
pA <- rbeta(M, p0 * (1 - Fst) / Fst, (1 - p0) * (1 - Fst) / Fst)  # each group drifts away
pB <- rbeta(M, p0 * (1 - Fst) / Fst, (1 - p0) * (1 - Fst) / Fst)
G <- matrix(0L, N, M)                            # genotypes: 0, 1 or 2 copies of the allele
for (h in 1:2) for (c in 1:22) {                 # two haplotypes per person
  z <- rnorm(N)
  for (j in which(chr == c)) {                   # correlated walk along the chromosome = LD
    if (j > min(which(chr == c))) z <- rho * z + sqrt(1 - rho^2) * rnorm(N)
    G[, j] <- G[, j] + (z < qnorm(ifelse(pop == 1, pB[j], pA[j])))
  }
}
causal <- sapply(c(2, 3, 5, 6, 8, 10, 11, 13, 16, 19), function(c) round(median(which(chr == c))))
OR <- c(1.10, 1.12, 1.15, 1.18, 1.20, 1.22, 1.25, 1.30, 1.35, 1.40)
eta <- -1.6 + 0.5 * pop + scale(G[, causal], scale = FALSE) %*% log(OR)  # B has more disease
y <- rbinom(N, 1, plogis(eta))                   # 1 = case

pcs <- irlba::prcomp_irlba(G, n = 4)$x           # top 4 principal components of the genotypes
pval <- function(g, cv) {                         # logistic regression, Wald test on the SNP
  f <- glm.fit(cbind(1, g, cv), y, family = binomial())
  z <- f$coefficients[2] / sqrt(chol2inv(f$qr$qr[1:f$rank, 1:f$rank])[2, 2])
  2 * pnorm(-abs(z))
}
p_raw <- apply(G, 2, pval, cv = NULL)            # no covariates
p_adj <- apply(G, 2, pval, cv = pcs)             # adjusted for 4 PCs
lambda <- function(p) median(qchisq(p, 1, lower.tail = FALSE)) / qchisq(0.5, 1)
cat(sprintf("%d SNPs, %d cases, %d controls\n", M, sum(y), N - sum(y)))
cat(sprintf("lambda: raw %.2f, PC-adjusted %.2f\n", lambda(p_raw), lambda(p_adj)))
cat("hits, raw:", which(p_raw < 5e-8), "\nhits, adjusted:", which(p_adj < 5e-8), "\ncausal:", causal, "\n")
```

which prints:

```
6000 SNPs, 2017 cases, 7983 controls
lambda: raw 1.92, PC-adjusted 1.09
hits, raw: 2571 2574 2575 4816 5420 5423 5430 5811
hits, adjusted: 4815 5420 5811
causal: 772 1258 2159 2574 3332 3996 4293 4815 5420 5811
```

The SNP numbers are positions along the simulated genome: 2574 is on chromosome 6, 4815 and 4816 on chromosome 13, 5420–5430 on chromosome 16 and 5811 on chromosome 19. Each run of `apply` fits 6,000 logistic regressions with `glm.fit`, the same model `glm(y ~ g + pcs, family = binomial)` would fit, without the overhead of building a formula 6,000 times.
